cues.en: Yeah, community not a project. You have to fund problem finding. This really drives funders crazy today. What do I mean by that? If you pick a problem too early, you might be picking it out of the current context. And therefore, you're going to be hampered unless you're incredibly lucky.

cues.en: So ARPA put a lot of money into just people dicking around with stuff. Milestones not deadlines. Baseball not golf. Meaning, when you lose a stroke in golf, you cry. cues.en: If you look at what we're funding, if we bat 350, we're going to change the world. That's what happened. Nobody cares about all the stuff that didn't work. cues.zh: 看看我们资助的东西，如果我们打击率 350，我们就会改变世界。事情就是这样。没人关心那些没成功的东西。有人说，那 65% 的失败呢？他们说，在棒球里那不叫失败，那叫必要开销。击球很难。当你在做非常非常难的事时，你没做好的那些时候，只是必要的开销。

cues.en: doing it the times you do well. And this is probably the biggest distinction that business people do not understand. cues.en: possible way, and I don't have time to really explain it. It's really interesting. People who are interested in this should write me an email. It didn't mean just other people. cues.zh: 可能的意义上，而我没时间真正解释它。这真的很有意思。对此感兴趣的人应该给我写邮件。它指的不只是其他人。它指的是其他软件、其他计算机。它指的是，当你把规模扩大时，沟通意味着什么。所以这个人是位大思想家。第九条，你不能在环城公路内思考。这当然指的是华盛顿特区，但这是一个普遍原则。他们问他为什么，他说……

cues.en: Well, because there's too much noise, there's too much politics, there's too much bullshit. And nobody does research in Washington DC. And so a solution to that was say, hey, let's not be here for longer than two years. And so every two years, so.
cues.zh: 嗯，因为那里噪音太多，政治太多，扯淡太多。而且华盛顿特区没人做研究。所以作为 ARPA 的资助者，我们最不想做的事，就是在那里思考。我们的工作是从政府那里拿钱，再把它发出去。所以一个解决办法就是，嘿，我们别在这里待超过两年。于是每两年，就……

cues.zh: “将军，如果您有要点要讲，您只有两分钟时间。”这句话大概是对 Ivan 最简洁的概括了。还有 Bob Taylor 和 Larry Roberts。正是这四个人促成了这一切。Taylor 之所以特别，是因为他也是建立 PARC 的人。而且他是 Licklider 的学生。Licklider 天赋异禀、直觉敏锐。Taylor 则是学习了 Licklider 身上那些精彩之处的学生。他能解释 Licklider 做的每一件事，以及为什么行得通。

cues.en: So here's a couple of things I'm not going to go on about, but basically the idea here is it isn't like let's look around and see what is available and what we can do with it. cues.zh: 模拟出那个东西。等你把软件调到满意了，再去设计一台计算机，把你在超级计算机上做的事情优化得更快、更高效。Sketchpad 就是这么来的。没人会觉得下一代图形系统要在一台跟这栋楼一样大的计算机上做出来，然后再量产一堆。所以在 ARPA 的几乎每个项目里，他们实际造出的数量都足以当作工具来用。它们可不只是演示品。

cues.en: And so part of this invention process had to require a kind of limited engineering. Park, for instance, had a thing where whatever you did, you had to make 100 of them. And you may start to edit the flow diagram. First, we erase a flow arrow, then move the connector out of the way so that we may draw a box in its place. The printing in the box is being used as commentary only in this case. The box is slightly too large.
cues.zh: 于是他们说，行吧，那我们就发明第一款平板电脑，体验跟你们今天用过的大多数平板一样好。这些人的特点就是，做出来的东西都足够出色。现在可以开始编辑流程图了。首先，我们擦掉一个流程箭头，然后移开连接线，以便在那个位置画一个方框。方框里的字在这里只作为注释。这个方框有点太大了。

cues.en: so we may change its size. Then draw a flow from the connector to the box. Attach a decision element to the box and draw a flow from it to scan. We then erase the flow. OK, so this is about 1968 or so. Again, on a big room-sized mainframe with one guy. But this system really...
cues.zh: 所以我们可以调整它的大小。接着从连接线画一条流向线到方框。在方框上附加一个判断元件，再从它引出一条流向线到 scan。然后我们擦除这条流向线。好，这大概是在 1968 年左右。同样是一个人面对一台房间那么大的大型机。但这套系统真的……

cues.en: You could ask your question more even about this. This system was one of the best systems I've ever used. It felt so intimate. It was so different from the mouse. It was one of the things that we actually looked at. I guess I do have to show the next thing here. Just so you think that VR wasn't something done recently, but the second thing Ivan did after he came back, the thing when he came back from ARPA was to do this.
cues.zh: 你甚至可以就这个多提几个问题。这套系统是我用过的最好的系统之一。它给人感觉非常亲切。它和鼠标完全不同。这也是我们实际参考过的东西之一。我想接下来这个我非展示不可了。好让你们知道 VR 并不是最近才有的东西，Ivan 从 ARPA 回来后做的第二件事就是这个。

cues.en: I worked on this when I was a graduate student. You could grab things that had a thing in your hand. You could grab things and move them around. It's a little exciting because instead of the thing that you're used to today in VR, it had two CRTs with 15,000 volts right above your ears crackling away. So it's a very exciting thing to do. And of course, one of the hardest things was to do good head positioning back then. There are many ways of...
cues.zh: 我读研究生的时候参与过这个项目。你可以手里拿着个设备来抓取物体。你可以抓住物体到处移动。这让人有点心跳加速，因为和你们今天习惯的 VR 设备不同，它是在你耳朵上方放了两个通着 15,000 伏高压、噼啪作响的 CRT 显示管。所以体验起来非常刺激。当然，当时最困难的事情之一就是做好头部定位。有很多种方法……

cues.en: One of the things they did here, I won't explain what it is, but it was hooked to a crane. So as you walked around this big room at MIT, a crane would automatically follow you with the positioning thing over your head to find out what this was about. And oh, man, I'm getting killed because I should stop right now. But I really have two more things to do. If you could give me two more minutes, I will do the first one here. This is something you have to think about.
cues.zh: 他们在这里做的一件事——我就不细解释是什么了——它是连在一个吊架上的。所以当你在 MIT 的这个大房间里走动时，头顶上带着定位装置的吊架会自动跟着你，来看看这是怎么回事。天呐，我要惨了，因为我现在该停下来了。但我真的还有两件事要讲。如果大家能再给我两分钟，我先讲这里的第一个。这是大家必须思考的一件事。

cues.en: Let time go one way and progress go the other way. Yay, boo, yay, boo. It goes up, it goes down. This is the way people tend to measure things. Problem is they never put in a threshold. If you put in a threshold, then the only things above the threshold count. Like if these are reading scores, nothing counts. Reading scores never get above threshold. So it doesn't matter whether they go up or down.
cues.zh: 假设时间是一条轴，进展是另一条轴。一会儿叫好，一会儿倒彩，起起落落。人们通常就是这么衡量事物的。问题是他们从不设立门槛。如果设了门槛，那就只有门槛之上的才算数。比如拿阅读成绩来说，那就全都不算数，因为阅读成绩从未跨过门槛。所以它们是涨是跌根本无所谓。

cues.en: What is actually needed changes over in time. You need more. And if you're measuring to a baseline, which people usually do, one of the ways of improving things or making it look like you're not doing such a bad job is to lower the baseline. For example, Apple completely lowered the baseline on what constitutes a reasonable user interface for iPhones and iPads. Interfaces on the systems beforehand had an undo and these don't. And I can name 15 more things.
cues.zh: 实际的需求是会随时间改变的，你需要得更多。如果你像人们通常那样对照基准线来衡量，那么“改进”现状或让自己显得没那么糟的办法之一，就是降低基准线。比如，Apple 彻底拉低了 iPhone 和 iPad 上“什么才算合理的用户界面”的基准线。以往系统上的界面都有撤销功能，而这些却没有。我还能再列出15条。

cues.en: Think about it. So what they did is they decided, well, we're just not going to work on all of those problems anymore. We're going to condition the unsophisticated public to work at the level of a two-year-old or a 92-year-old. And we're just going to eliminate everything in between. And the public has bought it because you don't want to count noses when you're looking for quality. People can be talked into anything.
cues.zh: 想想看。他们做的是干脆决定：好吧，我们再也不去解决所有这些问题了。我们要让没见过世面的大众习惯于两岁小孩或92岁老人的使用水平，直接砍掉介于两者之间的一切。公众还买账了，因为在追求品质时你可不能靠数人头来决定。人们是可以被忽悠着接受任何东西的。

cues.en: So what you have to do on this stuff is you have to pick something that is absolutely above that line. We call that in the McCready sweet spot. He's the guy who did man-powered flight. And once you have achieved that, it opens up a whole region that you can explore. And that's what we did at Park. The moonshot was set space travel back 50 years. Everybody uses this metaphor. We need a moonshot. No, we don't need a moonshot.
cues.zh: 所以在这种事情上，你必须挑选绝对在基准线之上的东西。我们称之为 McCready 甜点区。就是搞出人力飞行的那个人。一旦你达到了那个水准，就会开启一整片可供探索的新领域。我们在 PARC 做的事情正是如此。阿波罗登月计划让太空旅行倒退了50年。每个人都在套用这个隐喻：“我们需要登月计划。”不，我们不需要登月计划。

cues.en: You just don't do space travel with chemical rocketry. And what's interesting about the people who, like Jeff Bezos and, yeah, Elon, they don't get it. MV equals MV. Every child who read science fiction in the 50s knew this. What that means is you either have to carry a shitload of reaction mass with you if you're doing chemicals because you can't get the velocity high enough, so you have to put out a lot of mass.
cues.zh: 太空旅行根本不能靠化学火箭。有意思的是，像 Jeff Bezos，还有，对，Elon，他们都不懂这个。动量等于动量，MV 等于 MV。50年代每个读过科幻小说的孩子都知道这个道理。这意味着如果使用化学燃料，因为喷射速度无法提得足够高，你就必须喷出大量工质，导致你得随身携带巨量的反冲质量。

cues.en: And if you do that, you have to lift that mass. So you wind up with 45-story building rockets just to get into orbit. That is nuts. Anyway, I will not go on that. But the thing that was a tragedy was that there were very good proposals for how to get that high exhaust velocity using various forms of atomic power. And it was something that the public was not interested in. And the moonshot was not about space travel.
cues.zh: 而一旦这么做，你就必须把这些质量也送上天。结果就是，单单为了进入轨道，你就得造出45层楼高的火箭。这太荒唐了。总之，我就不多扯这个了。但悲剧在于，当年明明有极好的提案，可以利用各种形式的核动力来获得超高的喷气速度。公众却对此毫无兴趣。而当年的登月计划，根本就不是为了太空旅行。

cues.en: Okay, so I'll skip past this because I want to end with, oh yeah. So this tablet computer I thought up in 1968, it had two initial forms. One was the familiar tablet and the other one was what Ivan's head mounted display was inevitable with Moore's law. And then Nicholas Negroponte had this idea of wearing a watch and communicating with the rest of the world. Okay, so here's the last.
cues.zh: 好的，这部分我就跳过了，因为我想以……哦对了来收尾。我在1968年构想出的这台平板电脑，最初有两种形态。一种是我们熟悉的平板，另一种是与Ivan的头戴式显示器相配的形态——在摩尔定律下这都是必然的。后来Nicholas Negroponte提出了戴着手表与世界通信的想法。好，接下来是最后一部分。

cues.en: little segment and then I'll let you go. Wayne Gretzky, you know who Wayne Gretzky is. I'll bet. Greatest hockey player, whoever it is. And he was just a little guy. He tried to avoid fights. They asked him why he took so many shots on goal. He says, well, you miss 100% of the shots you don't take. So he wasn't trying to be careful. He scored more goals than anybody in history by a thousand.
cues.zh: 讲完这段就放大家走。Wayne Gretzky，你们应该知道Wayne Gretzky吧。我敢打赌你们知道。史上最伟大的冰球运动员。他个子很小，总是尽量避免冲突。有人问他为什么要那么多射门，他说："不射门，命中率就是百分之百。"所以他从不求稳。他的进球数比历史上任何人都多出一千个。

cues.en: So the fact that his percentage of misses was also high was irrelevant. And they asked him why he was better than anybody else. And he said, well, a good hockey player goes to where the puck is. A great one goes to where the puck is going to be. And he didn't mean tracking the puck. He meant getting into a place where somebody could pass him the puck where he could make a goal. So what he did is he looked at the entire configuration, saw where the future was going to be, and went to that place.
cues.zh: 所以他失误率也高这个事实根本无关紧要。有人问他为什么比别人强，他说："优秀的冰球运动员追着冰球跑，伟大的运动员奔向冰球将要到达的地方。"他说的不是盯着冰球，而是提前跑到一个位置，让队友能把球传给他、让他能射门。所以他做的是纵观全局，看清未来会怎样，然后赶到那个位置。

cues.en: So you can make a game to invent the future out of this. So you start off with a cosmic goodness intuition. Like for me, the tablet one was good. You identify a favorable exponential, like Moore's law. You take the cosmic intuition out 30 years, and you ask, can we say, wouldn't it be ridiculous if we didn't have this? And see, 30 years out, 30 years away, well, of course we'll have one. That's what that exponential means.
cues.zh: 由此你可以设计出一套"发明未来"的游戏。首先从一个宏大的美好直觉出发，比如对我来说，平板电脑就是那个直觉。然后找出一个有利的指数增长曲线，比如摩尔定律。把这个直觉外推30年，然后问自己：如果那时候我们还没有这东西，岂不是很荒谬？往远处看30年——当然会有，这就是指数增长的含义。

cues.en: And bring it back to the 10-15 year point. And at that point, you can just pay money, because that's also what Moore's Law and what Turing means, is if you pay a lot of money now, you can make the commodity computer of 10-15 years in the future. That's what the Alto was. It was about 50 times faster than what you got out of the time sharing terminal. And you make a bunch of them, and
cues.zh: 然后再拉回到10到15年这个时点。在这个时点，你只要花钱就行，因为这也是摩尔定律和图灵理论的意义所在：只要现在舍得砸钱，就能造出10到15年后的普及型计算机。Alto就是这样来的，它比当时的分时终端快了大约50倍。你造出一批这样的机器，

cues.en: You intertwine it with the, so run the software. And then you can do two kinds of computing in the future. One kind of computing is zillions of experiments to get a user interface that would be universal for now five billion people. And deal with millions of people that you've never, who are doing applications you've never seen before. And the other thing you can do, the thing on the right there is Microsoft Word as it was at Xerox PARC in 1974.
cues.zh: 再和软件结合起来运行。这样你就能在未来的两种计算方向上发力：一种是做无数实验，打造出如今50亿人通用的用户界面，并应对数百万你从未见过的、在使用你从未见过的应用的人。另一种是右边那个东西——1974年在施乐PARC时的Microsoft Word。

cues.en: If you optimize the code, you can get what the applications are going to be 10 years out. So those are the two things you can do by doing this supercomputer thing. And it costs money. In today's dollars, those altos cost about $125K apiece. And we made 2,000 of them. Think about that. Got to be a funder who's serious. Xerox went batshit when we did it. They really went batshit when we wanted to cash them in.
cues.zh: 如果你优化代码，就能看到应用在10年后会是什么样。所以做这个超级计算机项目，你能得到这两样东西。而这需要花钱。按今天的美元计算，那些Alto每台大约12.5万美元。我们造了2000台。想想看。得是认真的资助者才行。我们这么做的时候，施乐简直气疯了。当我们想兑现它们时，他们真的气疯了。

cues.en: But I'll just leave you this, since I'm over time now, I'll leave you this as one of the ways of escaping the present. Have a glimmer of an idea, take it so far out that you don't have to worry about how you're going to get there, and then you just bring it back. So instead of innovating out from the present, what you want to do is invent the future from the future. You go out and live in the future and bring the future back. Thank you.
cues.zh: 但既然我超时了，我就留给你们这个，作为逃离当下的一种方式。抓住一丝想法，把它推到很远，远到你不用担心怎么到达那里，然后再把它带回来。所以，不是从当下向外创新，你要做的是从未来发明未来。你走出去，活在未来，然后把未来带回来。谢谢。
